The most frequently reported top reason for using prediction markets was financial ("get rich") (52.54%), followed by prediction markets as a source of entertainment ("Makes watching games more fun") (22.70%). The least reported top motivations for using prediction markets were related to the features and qualities of prediction markets ("Has lines not available anywhere else") (4.32%) and competitive validation ("To make predictions and test my judgment against real-world outcomes.") (2.81%). Across all three motivations, 4.44% of responses were coded as invalid. For a complete list of themes for the three motivations participants reported, refer to Table 7.

When asked about motives for choosing prediction markets over sportsbooks, participants' most frequently reported top reason was preference for the experience that prediction markets provided ("It's easier to place bets on the same platform I'm already using") (36.58%), followed by financial gain ("Sometimes prediction markets offer better or higher chance of winning.") (26.98%). The least frequently reported top reasons were the lack of restrictions that prediction markets had over traditional sportsbooks ("sports betting is not legal where I live") (6.40%) and the perception that prediction markets were more trustworthy than other Sportsbook options ("They seem less risky") (5.56%). See Table 8 for a complete list of reported reasons for all three rankings. Across all three reasons, 23.49% (n = 662) of all responses were coded as invalid.

DISCUSSION

Prediction markets have grown rapidly in the past few years. Although they are currently regulated as a financial product (event contracts), it has been argued that they can be seen as a form of gambling (Andrade & Newall, 2025; Johnson & Chan, 2026). However, little is known about who uses prediction markets, their motivations, and links to traditional gambling. The present study addressed this gap. Taken together, our results provided support for our overall hypotheses that the convergence of prediction markets and gambling would extend beyond structural characteristics to gambling-related behaviours and psychological characteristics. In other words, prediction markets may be a form of gambling masquerading as a financial product.

In support of H1, sports betting was significantly more popular than each other category of event contracts, with over 80% of participants having traded sports contracts. These findings converge with market data, which suggest that sports contracts make up 78% of all trading volume on prediction markets (Kalshi; Radde, 2026). While the wisdom of the crowds has been argued to have some societal benefits as a way to form probability estimates of future economic events, population perceptions of arbitrary events, like who is going to win the Superbowl are of little consequence to the economy. Instead, the results of our study suggest that prediction markets primarily provide a different way to wager on sports. The majority of prediction market users (84.0%) in our sample also engaged in traditional gambling and this proportion was shown to be significantly greater than 50%, which supported H2. Furthermore, sports betting was the most commonly reported gambling activity. Notably, the present study was advertised as a study on financial behaviours rather than self-selecting for participants who used prediction markets or engaged in gambling and consequently, we did not self-select for sports bettors. Taken together, prediction markets appear to be primarily a vehicle for facilitating sports betting even in US states that have not legalised it.

Providing support for the aforementioned supposition, prediction markets were significantly more likely to be perceived to be a form of gambling (M = 8.27) rather than as a form of financial trading (M = 5.70; t(937) = 19.72, d = 0.64). This finding is notable given our sample consisted of participants who primarily engaged in all three activities and thus could provide a direct comparison of prediction markets to gambling and financial trading. The stock market is known by economists as a "positive sum" game, since the consequent spreading of risk across the economy can benefit both companies and individual investors. By comparison, both gambling and prediction markets are "zero sum" games, where one person can win only at another person's loss. Participants therefore appeared more aligned with economists in how they perceived prediction markets, rather than financial regulators who have classified prediction markets as financial transactions.

Our overall hypothesis (H3) that greater frequency of trading on frequency markets will resemble the demographic, psychological, and mental health and substance use patterns seen in sports betting was supported in several ways. Greater frequency prediction market use was significantly associated with being male, younger age, having a great financially focused selfconcept, impulsivity, psychological distress and substance use. These findings are not surprising given that sports betting was the most commonly traded event contract on prediction markets and the most commonly engaged form of gambling. Future research that examines whether prediction market users who trade on non-sporting events also demonstrate a similar behavioural and psychological profile to individuals who gamble would be highly informative.

In regards to gambling related risk and harms, our hypothesis (H4) was supported, with the exception of gambling fallacies. Specifically, greater frequency of trading on prediction markets was significantly associated with higher odds of problem gambling severity and lower dimensions of positive play (honesty, pre-commitment, personal responsibility and gambling literacy). The null effects regarding gambling fallacies have several potential explanations. First, the items used in this scale probe mistaken thoughts regarding conventional gambling products like slot machines and lottery tickets (Leonard & Williams, 2016), whereas we adapted the PPS to specifically probe behaviours and beliefs related to prediction markets. It may be that prediction markets promote unique fallacies compared to the fallacies involved in conventional gambling products. Second, while gambling fallacies have long been thought of as a key driver of problematic gambling, more recent longitudinal and experimental research has cast doubt on this causal relationship (Eben et al., 2026; Leonard et al., 2021).

Our exploratory results regarding motivations for trading on prediction markets further support the notion that they may be conceptualized as a form of gambling. Financial motivations were the most commonly endorsed reason for trading on prediction markets in both the quantitative and qualitative analyses. Financial motives are also a common motivation for engaging in gambling and have been robustly linked to problem gambling severity (Dias et al., 2026). Prediction markets also use similar advertisement tactics to traditional sports books such as financial incentives (e.g., sign-up bonus) to attract new users, further blurring the lines of gambling. Furthermore, financial motivations, in particular related to perceived rate or return or more favourable odds, were a commonly reported reason for choosing prediction markets over traditional sports books. Participants also drew direct parallels to gambling, noting that prediction markets fulfilled their pre-existing desires to gamble. In contrast, motivations for using prediction markets as a source of information (i.e., wisdom of the crowds) were less commonly mentioned than motivations that aligned with traditional gambling.

Our qualitative results clarified and extended the quantitative findings in numerous ways.

For example, participants consistently described financial gain as a top motivation for using prediction markets and perceived greater financial returns on prediction markets over other sports betting platforms, converging with the quantitative associations between a financially focused self-concept and more frequent trading. Second, participants described prediction markets as fulfilling a desire to gamble, aligning with the quantitative findings that most participants who used prediction markets also engaged in gambling. Such findings echo preliminary evidence that prediction market usage is associated with gambling (Mastromartino, 2026) and suggest that the psychological profile of those who use prediction markets aligns with those who also engage in gambling. Qualitative results also demonstrated additional nuance in the rationale of using prediction markets over traditional sportsbooks websites, with participants highlighting the variety of gambling options as a reason they specifically chose prediction markets, and describing prediction markets as having enhanced user interface and overall experience when compared to sportsbook. Despite this, quantitative results indicated that participants used prediction markets most frequently for sports betting. These findings suggest that the appeal of prediction markets may extend beyond the predominant categories that players bet on, and that prediction markets may be viewed as enhanced sports betting platforms in terms of their visual appeal and interface when compared to sportsbooks. For further information, see Table 9 for a comparison of the convergence and divergence between the quantitative and qualitative results.

Implications

These findings may have important implications for regulation and policy. Chiefly, though prediction markets position themselves as being a form of financial trading, users of prediction markets clearly understand them to be a type of gambling more than a type of financial trading. Prediction markets are legally accessible from the age of 18, whereas sports betting is legally available from the age of 21. Closing this regulatory gap is important given that young adults are at elevated risk of problematic gambling (Dellosa & Browne, 2024). In fact, 3.1% of our sample were under the age of 21, and the lack of restrictions related to age were mentioned as a motivation for engaging in prediction markets. Concerns around this appeal and accessibility to young people have been echoed in recent research (Chung, 2026). Prediction markets have also effectively facilitated sports betting in states that have not chosen to legalise it, and policymakers may also want to consider closing this regulatory loophole (Newall, 2026).

Additionally, prediction markets are not obligated to provide responsible gambling tools such as providing deposit limits, which again appears to be a consequential regulatory oversight given the findings reported here (Mastromartino, 2026). Indeed, individuals who self-exclude from traditional online gambling sites could then turn to prediction markets to place bets (Allyn, 2026b). Other measures that should be considered include the provision of warnings and information on prediction market adverts and platforms regarding the risk of problematic gambling.

Limitations

Several limitations are worth noting. The cross-sectional nature of the study precludes examining temporal links between prediction markets and traditional gambling. Future longitudinal studies that examine whether trading on prediction markets influences transition to traditional gambling or vice versa would be informative. Secondly, frequency and expenditure of both prediction market trading and gambling were assessed via retrospective self-reports, which may be susceptible to recall bias (Heirene et al., 2022). Replication of our results with objective data via account data or ecological momentary assessments would provide further confidence in these findings. Lastly, our sample was recruited from Prolific, which may limit generalizability of our results compared to population-representative samples (Pickering & Blaszczynski, 2021).

Conclusion

Prediction markets have made it possible for individuals to wager money on anything from the weather, politics, and sports, to how many times Elon Musk will post on X in a day.

This "gamblification" of life has raised concerns that prediction markets are a form of gambling in disguise (Andrade & Newall, 2025). Our results provide empirical support for this concern.

Specifically, prediction market users overlapped considerably in behaviours, motivations, psychological characteristics, and gambling-related risk and harms with individuals who gamble. Indeed, despite being regulated as a financial product, prediction market users perceive trading on event contracts to be a form of gambling more so than financial trading. Taken together, our results suggest that prediction markets could be considered a form of gambling in disguise and should be regulated as such. Table 9

Joint Display Table Quantitative Findings Qualitative Findings Interpretation A more financially focused selfconcept was associated with an increase in the odds of trading on prediction markets more frequently.

Participants consistently reported financial gain as a motivation for using prediction markets and noted the perceived increased financial gain that they received by using prediction markets over sports betting platforms.

Qualitative results were complementary to the quantitative findings, highlighting the importance of finances in the motivations and profile of those who use prediction markets. Most participants reported gambling in addition to trading on prediction markets.

Participants reported the desire to gamble as a motivation to use PMs, and that the lack of restrictions surrounding prediction markets allowed them to gamble in ways they were otherwise legally inaccessible to them.

Qualitative and quantitative results converged to demonstrate the relationship between prediction markets and gambling.

When asked about motivations for trading on prediction markets, the highest reported motivations were financial motives, followed by accomplishment and positive emotions.

Participants reported experiencing a "thrill" or positive sensations when using prediction markets, which served as a motivation for participants to engage in them. Participants also cited competitive validation, referring to instances where they felt satisfaction in being correct or accurate in their predictions, as a motivation to use prediction markets.

Quantitative and qualitative results converge to suggest that affective rewards, specifically positive emotions and a sense of accomplishment, are motivators for prediction market use.

Participants reported a variety of categories they traded on in prediction markets, including sports (81.20%), financial markets (55.2%), and domestic policies (41.8%).

Participants reported that their motivation for using prediction markets were due to the flexibility of betting options, most importantly, the ability to bet on different categories as a reason why they used prediction markets over traditional sports betting platforms.

Quantitative and qualitative findings diverged regarding the emphasis of sports betting. Although sports was the most frequently reported betting category quantitatively, qualitative findings highlighted the diversity of available betting options as a key motivation for choosing prediction markets over traditional sports betting platforms.

Quantitative Findings

Qualitative Findings Interpretation Participants most often used prediction markets to trade on sports event contracts.

Participants reported using prediction markets over traditional sports betting platforms due to a better user interface and experience.

Findings suggest that prediction markets may be viewed as elevated sports betting platforms and particularly attractive to individuals who wish to bet on sports.

The 10-item Gambling Fallacy Measure (GFM; Leonard & Williams, 2016) was used to assess endorsement of gambling fallacies (α = 0.70). Each item presents a gambling fallacy with multiple response options, but only a single correct answer. Lower scores indicate greater endorsement of gambling fallacies. Motivations for gambling were assessed using a parallel scale with the same items as the prediction market use motivation scale.

(α = 0.85). Higher scores indicate greater endorsement of a self-concept that is overly focused on financial success. The 20-item Short Impulsive Behaviour Scale (SUPPS-P; Cyders et al., 2014) was used to assess five facets of impulsivity (negative urgency [α = 0.82], positive urgency [α = 0.81], sensation-seeking [α = 0.80], lack of premeditation [α = 0.86], and lack of perseverance [α = 0.80]). Mean scores were used for each subscale with higher scores indicating greater endorsement of impulsive characteristics.
